title: Numbers With Repeated Digits
description: Brute force to optimized: checking every number directly versus combinatorially counting the complement (all-unique-digit numbers) and subtracting from n.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a positive integer n, return the count of numbers in the range [1, n] that have at least one repeated digit.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"At least one repeated digit\" is awkward to count directly","Count the COMPLEMENT instead: numbers with all unique digits, then subtract from n"],["Counting all-unique-digit numbers up to n is a classic digit-by-digit combinatorics problem","Handle shorter lengths with a direct permutation formula, and the same length as n digit by digit"]]}

blocks.text: Count how many numbers between 1 and n (inclusive) have some digit appearing more than once (for example, 22, 121, or 3223).

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting License Plates With a Repeated Digit
blocks.text: Picture counting how many license plate numbers up to some maximum value contain at least one repeated digit. It turns out easier to count the OPPOSITE, plates where every digit is different, and subtract that count from the total.

blocks.caption: Counting the complement (all-unique-digit numbers) is the easier direction

blocks.text: Only the number 11 (between 1 and 20) has a repeated digit, so the answer is 1.
262 numbers between 1 and 1000 have at least one repeated digit (1000 itself has three 0s, a repeat).
Before trying to directly count numbers WITH a repeated digit, notice it is far easier to count numbers WITHOUT any repeat, and subtract that count from n.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The count of numbers with at least one repeat, plus the count of numbers with all unique digits, together account for every number from 1 to n, so one can be derived from the other by subtracting from n.

Observation 2: Counting all-unique-digit numbers SHORTER than n's digit length is a direct permutation calculation: choose a nonzero first digit (9 choices), then choose each subsequent digit from whatever remains unused.

Observation 3: Counting all-unique-digit numbers with the SAME digit length as n, but not exceeding n, requires walking n's own digits one at a time, at each position counting how many valid (smaller, unused) digits could go there while keeping every digit before it fixed to match n exactly.

Observation 4: If n itself has all unique digits, it must be counted too, as the final valid number matching n exactly.

This leads to computing the count of all-unique-digit numbers up to n using permutation formulas (for shorter lengths) and a digit-by-digit walk (for the same length as n), then subtracting that count from n.
Check every number from 1 to n directly, testing whether its digits contain a repeat.

items: For every number from 1 to n, extract its digits.
Check whether any digit appears more than once.
Count every number where a repeat is found.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: check every number from 1 to n directly for a repeated digit

codes.python:
def num_dup_digits_at_most_n(n):
    count = 0
    for num in range(1, n + 1):              # check every number directly
        s = str(num)
        if len(set(s)) < len(s):
            count += 1
    return count

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every number from 1 to n is individually converted to its digits and checked for a repeat.
With n up to a billion, this direct enumeration becomes completely impractical.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times digits of n), checking every number individually.
Space: O(digits of n) per check.
Limitation: with n up to a billion, iterating over every single number is far too slow; a purely combinatorial approach is required.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why counting "has a repeat" directly is hard: there is no simple combinatorial formula for this condition directly.

What is easier to count: numbers with ALL UNIQUE digits, since choosing digits one at a time with no repeats is a standard permutation count.

How to count unique-digit numbers shorter than n: for each shorter length, choose a nonzero first digit (9 options), then choose the remaining digits as a permutation of the remaining 9 digits.

How to count unique-digit numbers the SAME length as n, but not exceeding it: walk n's digits one position at a time; at each position, count how many smaller, still-unused digits could be placed there (with the digits before it fixed to match n), permuting the remaining positions freely; stop early the moment n itself repeats a digit.

The core idea: compute the total count of unique-digit numbers up to n combinatorially, then the answer is n minus that count.

Sum the count of all-unique-digit numbers for every digit-length shorter than n's using direct permutation formulas. Then walk n's own digits one at a time, at each position counting valid smaller unused digits (permuting the remaining positions), stopping early if n repeats a digit itself, and add 1 if n's own digits are all unique. Subtract this total from n for the final answer.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: count unique-digit numbers combinatorially, subtract from n

blocks.text: Every number from 1 to n either has all unique digits or has a repeat, so counting the unique-digit ones combinatorially and subtracting from n gives exactly the repeat count. Shorter-length numbers are counted with a direct permutation formula (choose a nonzero first digit, then permute the rest). Numbers with the same length as n are counted by walking its digits, at each position counting smaller unused digits that could legally appear there while everything before stays fixed to match n, correctly enumerating every unique-digit number up to and including n itself.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(digits of n), a small constant number of positions to walk through.
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: This is a classic "count the complement" problem: directly counting numbers with a repeated digit is awkward, but counting all-unique-digit numbers has a clean combinatorial structure, computed with permutation formulas for shorter lengths and a digit-by-digit walk for numbers matching n's own length.

items: Allowing a leading zero when counting the first digit of a number, which is never valid.
Forgetting to stop early once n itself is found to repeat a digit while walking its digits.
Forgetting to add 1 for n itself when its own digits happen to all be unique.

blocks.text: Stating the complement strategy explicitly, "count all-unique-digit numbers, then subtract from n," is the key reframing that turns an awkward direct count into a clean combinatorial one.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "n can be up to a billion, how do you avoid checking every number", think: count the complement (all-unique-digit numbers) combinatorially, then subtract from n.

Digit DP, a broader technique for counting numbers up to n satisfying some digit-based property, walking digits one position at a time.
Any "count the complement" problem where the opposite condition is easier to count directly.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n times digits of n) time. The optimized combinatorial approach runs in O(digits of n) time and O(1) space, independent of n's actual size.

items: Pattern: counting the complement (all-unique-digit numbers) combinatorially, using permutations and a digit-by-digit walk.

Core Idea: the answer is n minus the count of all-unique-digit numbers up to n, computed with direct permutation formulas for shorter lengths and a careful digit walk for numbers matching n's own length.
Time: O(n times digits of n) for the brute force, O(digits of n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(digits of n) for the brute force, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: counting the complement (unique digits) combinatorially is far easier than counting "has a repeat" directly.
Interview Difficulty: a classic digit-DP-style counting problem; the digit-walk logic requires careful, precise bookkeeping.
One line memory trick: n minus the count of all-unique-digit numbers up to n.
